titre: The Jazz Singer has only two minutes of dialogue
accroche: The film credited with inventing talking pictures is mostly a silent film with songs. Its spoken lines add up to two minutes.
contenu_vulgarise:
On October 6, 1927, The Jazz Singer opens in just two theaters. Audiences discover Al Jolson singing at the top of his lungs, then, between songs, speaking lines that can actually be heard. Legend has it that silent cinema expired that night.

The film itself is mostly silent. Ron Hutchinson, in the essay the Library of Congress publishes on the film, writes that it is in fact “largely silent,” with music and sound effects in those passages, and that there are only two minutes of real dialogue. Only one scene contains any, the one where Jolson jokes with his mother, played by Eugenie Besserer. His lines about a move to the Bronx are not in the script: he most likely improvised them.

## A film of songs, not of lines

The process used is Warner Bros.' Vitaphone. A single motor drives the projector and a 16-inch disc, which carries the soundtrack. Sam Warner, blown away by the Bell Labs demonstration in 1925, first sees it as a way of giving theaters that show silent films a full orchestra, not of making actors talk. The first Vitaphone feature, Don Juan, in 1926, contains only music and sound effects. It is the audience's reaction to the sung and spoken short films that precede the feature that reverses the strategy: viewers want to hear singing and talking.

The Jazz Singer is therefore not the first talking picture, and the Library of Congress essay says so from its opening words: it is not the first, nor even the thousandth. Dozens of processes for synchronizing sound and image are developed from 1896 on, and fail right away. The first all-talking feature is Lights of New York, in 1928, which costs Warner $23,000 and earns more than a million. Yet it isn't seen as the birth certificate of talking pictures.

## What the film really did

What The Jazz Singer demonstrates is a market. Made for $422,000, it plays in 235 theaters in March 1928, the only feature then in which dialogue and singing can be heard, and it had earned two million dollars by 1931. Jolson's next film, The Singing Fool (1928), costs less but contains far more dialogue, and earns four million. Hutchinson ties Warner's expansion to this success, as the company buys hundreds of theaters, along with the studio's decision to offer all its films from then on with a synchronized Vitaphone accompaniment; for him, by the end of 1929, silent film is dead.

The Academy, for its part, does not treat the film as an ordinary contender. At the first ceremony, in 1929, it is ruled ineligible for the two main prizes, according to Wikipedia, and Warner Bros. receives a special award for producing what the Academy calls “the pioneer outstanding talking picture.”

One shift remains: of a revolution we usually remember the work that symbolizes it, when that work has often done no more than make visible what had been in the making for years, elsewhere and quietly.

repere.texte: At its premiere on October 6, 1927, The Jazz Singer is “largely silent” according to Ron Hutchinson, with music and sound effects; it has only two minutes of actual dialogue. Cost: $422,000; earnings in 1931: two million.
repere.source: Ron Hutchinson, “The Jazz Singer,” Library of Congress (National Film Registry)

carte.punch: The film that “invented talking pictures” has two minutes of dialogue.
carte.idee: The Jazz Singer (1927) is mostly a silent film with music: only one scene contains real dialogue, two minutes in all. It isn't the first talkie, but it proves that audiences will pay to hear.

pour_aller_plus_loin.note: Two pages on Vitaphone technology, the shoot in the summer of 1927 and the box-office figures.

quiz.question: Why is The Jazz Singer not strictly speaking “the first talking picture”?
choix: Because its sound process was pulled from the market by rival studios only weeks after its theatrical release
Because its soundtrack was recorded after the shoot by dubbing artists, not by the actors themselves on set
Because synchronized-sound systems already existed and it contains only two minutes of dialogue, the rest being music
Because its dialogue was added afterward, in a 1931 reissue, the premiere version being entirely silent
quiz.explication: According to the Library of Congress, the film is largely silent, with music and sound effects, and has only two minutes of real dialogue as of its premiere on October 6, 1927. Dozens of synchronization systems had failed since 1896, and the first all-talking feature is Lights of New York (1928). Vitaphone was not pulled: Warner extends it to all its films, and the film's songs and dialogue were recorded during the shoot, not dubbed.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What leads Warner Bros. to make actors talk, when Vitaphone had not been designed for that?
choix: The audience's reaction to the sung and spoken short films shown before the feature
A contractual demand imposed by Al Jolson before he accepted the role
A trade-press article faulting Warner for lagging behind Paramount
The bankruptcy of the competitor that produced Don Juan, forcing Warner to innovate
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Sam Warner saw Vitaphone as a way of providing orchestral accompaniment to theaters, not of making actors talk: it is the audience's reaction to the sung and spoken short films shown before the feature that changes the strategy.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Which scene contains the two minutes of real dialogue in The Jazz Singer?
choix: A breakup scene between Jolson and his fiancée, added in the final edit
The scene where Jolson jokes with his mother, played by Eugenie Besserer, about a move to the Bronx
The thank-you speech Jolson improvises before the theater audience, at the end of the film
A scene between Jolson and his manager, cut from the restored version
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The Library of Congress essay places the only real dialogue in the scene with Eugenie Besserer, where Jolson improvises lines about a move to the Bronx that are not in the script.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does Don Juan, the first feature released with the Vitaphone process in 1926, contain?
choix: It already contains two hours of synchronized dialogue, well before The Jazz Singer
It was pulled from theaters after a commercial failure that set Vitaphone back a year
It contains only music and sound effects, with no dialogue at all
It was shot at the same time as The Jazz Singer, by the same technical crew
quiz_supplementaire.explication: According to Ron Hutchinson's essay, Don Juan (1926), the first Vitaphone feature, has only music and sound effects, with no dialogue, Warner then seeing it as an orchestral accompaniment for theaters.
